name: LGD-4033

lead: LGD-4033 (ligandrol) is an oral selective androgen receptor modulator that lifters take to add lean mass and a bigger, more muscular physique within weeks, with less perceived hormonal impact than steroids.

It activates the androgen receptor in muscle and bone and suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. A randomised phase I trial in 76 healthy men found 21 days raised lean body mass, and a phase 2 trial after hip fracture reported dose-dependent lean-mass gains. In those trials, testosterone and HDL cholesterol fell.

paras: Sold online as a research chemical and taken orally for several weeks, often during bulks and sometimes with post-cycle support. Users report strength and fullness changes within the first weeks.

Not approved and banned in sport. Documented problems include testosterone suppression, reduced HDL cholesterol and drug-induced liver injury, especially at amounts above trial levels. Product contents are unreliable.

angle.text: LGD-4033 is a SARM used by lifters to add lean mass in a few weeks with less perceived hormonal impact than steroids. It activates the androgen receptor in muscle for a bigger, more muscular look. Small trials in older and young men showed lean-mass gains alongside hormonal suppression and lipid changes.

lead: LGD-4033, also called Ligandrol and by the developmental code VK5211, is an orally taken, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) originally developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals. It has been studied for muscle atrophy, including after hip fracture, and was also explored for cachexia, hypogonadism and osteoporosis; it is not approved for any medical use.[1]

For appearance, the draw is lean mass. SARMs are designed to switch on androgen receptors in muscle and bone with weaker activity in tissues such as the prostate, and people who use LGD-4033 outside medicine do so hoping for a more muscular, leaner physique from the same training, often as a substitute or adjunct for anabolic steroids.[1][2][3] In a randomised phase I trial in 76 healthy men, 21 days of LGD-4033 was well tolerated and raised lean body mass, and a phase 2 trial in people recovering from hip fracture reported dose-dependent increases in lean mass.[4][1]

The compound has far fewer published human studies than the SARM enobosarm, with only four small clinical studies reported as of 2023 according to Wikipedia.[1] It is sold online as a research chemical and discussed on bodybuilding forums. Published concerns include dose-dependent drops in testosterone and HDL cholesterol in trials, multiple case reports of drug-induced liver injury in non-medical users, and a JAMA analysis of products sold online as SARMs that examined their composition and labelling.[1][5][6][7] The compound is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list, and several athletes have been sanctioned after positive tests.[1][8]
infobox: Ligand Pharmaceuticals; licensed to Viking Therapeutics in 2014[1]
Investigational (US); not approved; prohibited in sport
Phase I in 76 healthy men (2013); phase 2 in 108 hip-fracture patients (began 2016)[1][4]

paras: LGD-4033 is a small, lipophilic, orally active molecule that binds the androgen receptor with high affinity and was developed to produce muscle and bone effects with less stimulation of the prostate than testosterone.[1] It is one of the most commonly used non-medical SARMs alongside enobosarm (ostarine), andarine and RAD140 (vosilasarm).[1][3]

The SARM class is not approved by the FDA or European Medicines Agency; as of 2023 no SARM had been approved, and Australia classifies them as prescription-only (S4).[3] Enobosarm is the most-studied of the class and has been tested in phase 2 and 3 trials, including in cancer-related muscle wasting, where it improved lean mass but not strength in two phase 3 trials reported in 2013.[9][10]

The first nonsteroidal androgen-receptor agonists were developed in 1998 by two groups independently: the University of Tennessee and Ligand Pharmaceuticals, which worked on a quinolone core.[3] The term "SARM" was introduced by David Negro-Vilar in 1999, modelled on selective estrogen receptor modulators, and endocrinologist David Handelsman has criticised it as marketing rather than pharmacology.[3]

The mechanism of tissue selectivity was still debated as of 2020: proposals include absence of 5-alpha-reductase activation, tissue-specific coactivator and corepressor ratios, and non-genomic signalling through membrane-associated receptors, while autoradiography studies show no preferential distribution to anabolic tissues.[3]

LGD-4033 is not approved for any medical use. Wikipedia reports that as of 2023 it was in phase 2 development by Viking Therapeutics for muscle atrophy in people with hip fracture, while development for cachexia, hypogonadism and osteoporosis was discontinued.[1]

The compound is sold by online vendors for physique and performance purposes, and Wikipedia states it is often used at doses far above those tested in clinical trials, with unknown effectiveness and safety; it also notes that social media has played an important role in spreading non-medical SARM use.[1] On T Nation, users describe taking it in cycles for periods of weeks, sometimes alongside the growth-hormone secretagogue MK-677, as a substitute or adjunct in relation to anabolic steroids, or after prohormone use.[2][11][12] Others discuss using SARMs during post-cycle recovery.[13]

SARM use in this setting is promoted on social media, and Wikipedia reports that recreational doses often exceed trial doses and that fat-free mass gains are generally lower than those from moderate testosterone doses.[1][3] In a user survey summarised there, most respondents were satisfied and a majority would use SARMs again, though most also reported adverse effects.[3]

In the 21-day phase I trial, 1 mg per day increased lean body mass by about 1.2 kg compared with baseline, according to Wikipedia, which compares this with a 1.3 kg gain seen with enobosarm in 12 weeks in older adults.[1] The 2013 report in The Journals of Gerontology described dose-proportional pharmacokinetics, a long half-life, and no drug-related serious adverse events.[4]

In the 12-week phase 2 trial in 108 men and women after hip fracture surgery, Wikipedia reports placebo-adjusted lean body mass gains of 4.8 percent at 0.5 mg per day, 7.2 percent at 1 mg per day and 9.1 percent at 2 mg per day, with dose-dependent muscle strength improvements and reported tolerability.[1]

A 2025 systematic review of randomised trials of SARMs on physical performance pooled nine studies of six SARMs, including LGD-4033, with 970 patients and a mean follow-up of 80 days.[14] A 2013 review of SARMs for cancer-related muscle wasting described enobosarm as the most clinically characterised SARM and reviewed LGD-4033 data alongside it.[10]

Human trials are few. The multi-dose phase I study enrolled 76 healthy men aged 21 to 50 randomised to placebo or 0.1, 0.3 or 1.0 mg daily for 21 days; it measured lean and fat mass, strength, stair-climbing power, hormones, lipids, PSA and liver enzymes. Hemoglobin, PSA, AST, ALT and QT intervals did not change significantly, and the drug was well tolerated.[4] Hormonal and lipid effects reported by Wikipedia from the clinical program include dose-dependent decreases in total and free testosterone, FSH, SHBG, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, with LH, total cholesterol, LDL and PSA unchanged.[1]

A phase 2 trial begun in November 2016 enrolled 108 people recovering from hip fracture surgery, as described above.[1] A published case report on a man using LGD-4033 together with MK-677 examined body composition, circulating biomarkers and muscle androgen hormone and receptor content.[15]
Wikipedia lists three small phase I trials and one phase 2 trial as the total of reported clinical studies.[1] No clinical trial has tested LGD-4033 at the higher doses used by non-medical users.

Reported effects in trials include headache and dry mouth, lowered HDL cholesterol and testosterone, and lowered SHBG.[1] Because HDL falls relative to LDL, Wikipedia says LGD-4033 could theoretically raise the risk of heart attack and stroke; the US FDA states that liver toxicity, adverse blood lipid effects and potential cardiovascular risk are among the potential harms of SARMs.[1] Liver enzyme elevations were not reported in the small trials, but several case reports of drug-induced liver injury in non-medical users have been published, including a 32-year-old man with cholestatic hepatitis confirmed on biopsy, a 2023 German report, and a 2024 case report.[1][16][17][6] A review of two cases of SARM- and post-cycle-therapy-related liver injury discusses the broader literature.[18]

Masculinising effects in women are largely uncharacterised, and Wikipedia notes anecdotal reports of masculinisation with black-market SARMs in online forums.[1] A T Nation poster described a long hormonal slump after cycling SARMs including LGD-4033, and another said he felt unwell by the fourth week and wondered whether the product was actually a prohormone.[19][12]

LGD-4033 binds the androgen receptor with high affinity (Ki about 0.9 nM) and little affinity for progesterone, glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid receptors.[1] In castrated rats it increased levator ani muscle weight to around 140 percent of intact controls, while prostate weight reached about 45 percent, a pattern researchers describe as tissue selectivity.[1] Androgen receptor activation also feeds back on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which is the proposed explanation for falling testosterone levels.[4][5]

Pharmacokinetics were linear across 0.1 to 1 mg daily, with about threefold accumulation over 21 days and an elimination half-life of 24 to 36 hours.[1][4] Human metabolism and excretion studies, done mainly for doping control, have identified multiple metabolites in urine.[20][21]

LGD-4033 is a nonsteroidal pyrrolidinyl-benzonitrile SARM (molecular weight about 338 g/mol), sometimes called a quinoline-type SARM because of its predecessor LG121071. Its structure had not been disclosed as late as 2013, and it is distinct from the other Ligand compounds LGD-2226, LGD-2941 and LGD-3303.[1]

Ligand Pharmaceuticals discovered LG121071, the first orally active nonsteroidal androgen receptor agonist, described in 1999; LGD-4033 followed and was first described in the literature in 2010, with phase I trials beginning in 2009.[1] A multi-dose phase I report appeared in 2013, and a phase 2 trial in muscle wasting began in November 2016 with results reported in 2017 and 2018.[1][4] Viking Therapeutics licensed the compound from Ligand on 22 May 2014.[1]

Proponents describe LGD-4033 as among the strongest SARMs for lean mass and strength and as a way to gain without the full range of steroid side effects; they commonly pair it with other SARMs or with MK-677 and describe the effects in training logs.[2][11][22] Some users treat SARMs as a bridge during or after steroid cycles.[13]

Others in the same forums stress hormonal slumps, lipid changes and the possibility of mislabelled products, and several describe feeling unwell or finding their bloodwork changed.[19][12][23] This split between enthusiasm and caution is the usual pattern in SARM threads.

Coverage of SARMs has focused on gray-market sales, mislabelled products and athlete doping cases. The FDA warned two US supplement companies on 23 October 2017, Infantry Labs of Missouri and Panther Sports Nutrition of New Jersey, over products containing LGD-4033 marketed as supplements.[1] Marketing SARMs for human consumption has led to criminal convictions in the US, and Australia imposed its largest-ever Therapeutic Goods Act fine for SARM-related violations, according to Wikipedia.[3]

A 2017 JAMA study by researchers who purchased products sold online as SARMs analysed their contents against labels, motivated by reports of increasing use of unapproved SARMs to enhance appearance and performance.[7] A German analysis of black-market products from 2010 to 2013 likewise examined products that could be doping agents.[24]

Other SARMs discussed alongside LGD-4033 include enobosarm, RAD140, andarine and YK-11.[3] LGD-4033 is often discussed with the growth-hormone secretagogue MK-677 and with anabolic steroids, and T Nation threads treat it in relation to oral steroids and post-cycle therapy.[2][12][25]

In the United States LGD-4033 is an investigational new drug. In October 2017 the FDA warned a Missouri supplement company that distributing LGD-4033 products violated the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, because they were marketed as dietary supplements though they would be new drugs.[1] SARMs were added to the WADA Prohibited List in 2008, and LGD-4033 has been reported in athlete urine samples and supplements; Wikipedia lists several athletes with positive tests, some of whom deny knowingly taking it.[1][8][26]

Reported cases listed by Wikipedia include American football quarterback Will Grier (suspended in 2015, a result the university disputed), NBA player Joakim Noah (20-game ban in 2017), Australian swimmer Shayna Jack (2019, who said she did not knowingly take it), Canadian canoeist Laurence Vincent-Lapointe (positive in 2019, cleared in January 2020 after an account of exposure via a partner), tennis player Nicolas Jarry (2020, who blamed contaminated vitamins) and NBA player Tristan Thompson (25-game suspension in January 2024 for LGD-4033 and ibutamoren).[1] The first adverse analytical finding for a SARM was reported in 2010, and enobosarm and LGD-4033 are the most commonly detected.[3] Metabolite studies for doping control have shown that urine contains multiple metabolites, and supplements can contain LGD-4033 as an ingredient or as a contaminant.[21][26]

Wikipedia states that many products sold online as LGD-4033 contain none of it or contain unrelated substances, and doses are often not as labelled.[1] A 2017 JAMA study and a German study of black-market products from 2010 to 2013 examined the identity of such products.[7][24]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Forum discussion on T Nation includes a user who ordered about eleven SARMs to run together, a poster who described LGD-4033 as a very suppressive SARM, a user who reported an 8-week run followed by blood work, and a poster who said low doses appeared to harm HDL/LDL ratios.[22][19][11][23] Other posts treat it as the SARM equivalent of a particular oral steroid, or cite the 2013 phase I paper in an argument about safety.[25][27]

lore.intro: On forums LGD-4033 is treated as one of the stronger and more suppressive SARMs, used in cycles and often combined with other compounds.[19][22]
